title: How Retailers Can Reinvent the Digital Flywheel for Agentic Commerce
gist: BCG argues external AI agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) threaten the visit-driven retail flywheel of marketplaces, loyalty/personalization and retail media, with US AI-driven traffic possibly overtaking organic search by 2028 and over half of e-commerce agent-assisted by 2030. Retailers must win both a 'destination' game (direct visits, protected customer data) and an 'evaluation' game (agent recommendations on price, availability, delivery), sharing product data but not customer data; only 18% say their marketplaces are agent-ready, and agent intermediaries will likely eventually charge OTA-style tolls.

insights.claim: BCG's survey of 50 of the top 300 global retailers found marketplaces account for 26% of online GMV on average (35% in the top quartile), and new marketplace customers generate 23% of retailer traffic (30% in the top quartile).
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Third-party marketplaces are now a quarter-plus of leading retailers' online GMV, making marketplace scale a core valuation driver for omnichannel retailers.
insights.quote: Marketplaces account for 26% of these retailers’ total online gross merchandise value (GMV), on average, rising to 35% among the top quartile.
insights.locator: The Digital Flywheel Already Drives Retail Growth

insights.claim: Loyalty and personalization programs account for an attributed 11% of surveyed retailers' GMV on average, rising to 15% in the top quartile.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Loyalty-attributed GMV is the part of the flywheel most at risk if agent-referred purchases stay anonymous.
insights.quote: Loyalty and personalization programs account for an attributed 11% of retailers’ GMV, on average, rising to 15% among the top quartile.
insights.locator: The Digital Flywheel Already Drives Retail Growth

insights.claim: Retail media draws an average of 28% of its revenue from third-party marketplace sellers (42% in the top quartile), and 95% of retailers see retail media as a major source of future profit growth.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retail media profit is tightly coupled to marketplace seller density; marketplace disruption by agents would hit the highest-margin line.
insights.quote: Ninety-five percent of retailers see retail media as a major source of future profit growth.
insights.locator: The Digital Flywheel Already Drives Retail Growth

insights.claim: The digital flywheel is a self-reinforcing system: marketplaces expand assortment without inventory and generate shopping data, that data powers personalization and loyalty, the resulting traffic supports high-margin retail media, and media profits fund further investment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retailers running all four components (Amazon/Tmall model; Walmart, Target, Lowe’s, Kingfisher, Tesco building) have compounding economics that point solutions lack.
insights.quote: Together, they form the digital flywheel.
insights.locator: A shopper opens an AI assistant

insights.claim: Lowe’s digital commerce head argues marketplace and media network are mutually dependent: neither can scale without the other because assortment drives traffic and traffic drives ad return.
insights.speaker: Joe Cano
insights.so_what: Retailers with a media network but no marketplace (or vice versa) face a structural scale ceiling.
insights.quote: You can’t scale a marketplace without a media network, and you can’t scale a media network without a marketplace.
insights.locator: Joe Cano, senior vice president

insights.claim: Retailers that got the flywheel right over the past ten years earned higher growth, profitability, and valuation multiples.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Flywheel completeness is offered as an explanation for retail valuation dispersion.
insights.quote: Retailers that got the flywheel right over the past ten years earned higher growth, profitability, and valuation multiples.
insights.locator: Retailers that got the flywheel right

insights.claim: External AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini increasingly sit between retailers and shoppers, so a retailer can make a sale without ever receiving a site visit, undermining a visit-dependent growth model.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Traffic-based KPIs and onsite ad inventory become less reliable leading indicators for e-commerce retailers.
insights.quote: In agentic commerce, a retailer can make a sale and never receive a visit.
insights.locator: A shopper opens an AI assistant

insights.claim: Referrals from external agents were under 1% of website visits for leading European brands and retailers in late 2025 but could reach 5% by end-2026, and including untracked post-agent direct visits, agents' real traffic effect can be up to four times the referral figure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reported AI referral share materially understates agent influence; a 5% referral share may imply up to ~20% agent-shaped traffic.
insights.quote: With those visits included, agents’ effect on website traffic can be up to four times the referral figure.
insights.locator: BCG’s analysis of leading European brands

insights.claim: In the US, AI-driven traffic to retail websites could overtake organic search traffic as early as 2028.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Signals a shift in digital acquisition spend from SEO/paid search toward agent visibility; negative read for search-dependent traffic models.
insights.quote: AI-driven traffic could overtake organic search traffic by as early as 2028
insights.locator: BCG’s analysis of leading European brands

insights.claim: 81% of US consumers and 53% in Europe expect to use AI agents when shopping, and more than half of e-commerce spending could be agent-assisted by 2030.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sizes the agent-assisted share of e-commerce as a majority within roughly four years, with the US ahead of Europe.
insights.quote: By 2030, more than half of e-commerce spending could be agent-assisted.
insights.locator: Agentic commerce remains at an early stage.

insights.claim: Only 4% of consumers would let an agent complete a purchase on its own, even as shopping-related generative AI use rose 35% in nine months and over 60% of consumers trust what it tells them, so the current battleground is the recommendation, not the transaction.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Agentic checkout hype is premature; near-term value accrues to whoever controls the recommendation layer rather than payment/checkout.
insights.quote: The battleground today is the recommendation, not the transaction.
insights.locator: Retailers Play Two Games, Destination and Evaluation

insights.claim: Disintermediation risk is greatest in low-consideration categories like household consumables and repeat orders, which are easiest to delegate, while fashion, beauty, and luxury are less exposed because discovery matters more.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Grocery/consumables-heavy retailers face more agent-driven commoditization than discovery-led fashion and luxury players.
insights.quote: The risk is greatest in low-consideration categories such as household consumables and repeat orders, which are easiest to delegate.
insights.locator: The destination game matters because

insights.claim: Agent-routed demand is unlikely to stay free: every online intermediary between retailers and shoppers eventually charged for position, as comparison sites and paid search did and as online travel agencies now take roughly 15% to 25% of each booking.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Model a future agent take-rate into retail margins; AI platforms have an obvious path to a toll on commerce.
insights.quote: online travel agencies now take roughly 15% to 25% of each booking
insights.locator: Agent-routed demand is also unlikely to stay free.

insights.claim: Retailers that keep building only for human shoppers risk agents standing between them and customers, eventually becoming interchangeable, margin-compressed fulfillment nodes.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies a widening valuation split between agent-ready retailers and laggards that get commoditized.
insights.quote: become interchangeable, margin-compressed fulfillment nodes
insights.locator: Retailers in the second group could find agents

insights.claim: Retailers must play two games at once: a destination game to win direct shopper visits (preserving customer data and onsite media) and an evaluation game to win the agent's recommendation on product data, price, availability, delivery, returns, and offers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A lens for assessing retailer strategy: strength in one game does not guarantee the other.
insights.quote: Competing for the visit is a destination game, in which retailers give shoppers reasons to shop with them directly.
insights.locator: Retailers Play Two Games, Destination and Evaluation

insights.claim: Agents create a trust feedback loop: a shopper may instruct an agent to prefer a trusted retailer, but if that retailer underperforms on agent-evaluated criteria the agent may recommend alternatives, eroding the shopper's trust and future instructions.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Brand loyalty becomes contingent on machine-measurable execution, raising churn risk for retailers with weak price or delivery.
insights.quote: If the retailer falls short, the agent may recommend alternatives, influencing both the shopper’s trust and future instructions.
insights.locator: Agents also create a new feedback loop for trust.

insights.claim: Losing the customer relationship is retailers' top concern about agentic commerce, cited by 91% of respondents.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retailers are likely to resist full data openness, shaping how fast AI platforms can build commerce layers.
insights.quote: Losing the customer relationship is retailers’ most common concern, cited by 91% of respondents.
insights.locator: The destination game matters because

insights.claim: Hotels offer the model: they use travel websites for reach while investing in direct booking, member rates, and loyalty to keep their highest-value repeat guests in owned channels.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retailer-agent economics may converge on the hotel-OTA equilibrium: intermediary for acquisition, owned channel for repeat high-value customers.
insights.locator: Hotels provide a useful model.

insights.claim: Retailers are building their own shopping agents to strengthen the destination, including Amazon's Alexa for Shopping, Walmart's Sparky, Lowe’s Mylow, and Instacart's Clementine, while bol embedded its agent throughout the shopping journey rather than as a parallel gateway.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retailer-owned agents are a defensive bet to keep conversational discovery and its ad inventory onsite.
insights.locator: Retailers need the same balance.

insights.claim: Bol, which launched its shopping agent in September 2026 with retail media built in from day one, limits external agents to discovery and does not plan to take the transaction offsite.
insights.speaker: Joris Scheepens
insights.so_what: Shows a retailer posture that captures agent reach while ring-fencing checkout and the customer relationship.
insights.quote: We don’t plan to take the transaction offsite.
insights.locator: Bol Builds Its Own Agent into the Customer Journey

insights.claim: Nordstrom pursued a staged approach: prioritizing visibility on external AI platforms and AI-assisted onsite discovery, building agentic checkout but holding it until demand warrants, and deprioritizing a dedicated in-ChatGPT presence because other attempts had not shown compelling results.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: In-platform storefronts inside AI assistants have not yet proven out; product-feed visibility is the near-term win.
insights.quote: The fourth opportunity, a dedicated presence inside a platform such as ChatGPT, isn’t a current priority, as other industry attempts have yet to show compelling results.
insights.locator: Nordstrom Tests, Learns, and Stays Ready

insights.claim: Nordstrom's own shopping agent shows meaningfully higher conversion among users, though the company cautions this may partly reflect selection bias.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Treat retailer-reported AI-agent conversion uplifts skeptically; self-selection inflates them.
insights.quote: though Nordstrom cautions the results may partly reflect selection bias
insights.locator: To support agent-assisted discovery on its website

insights.claim: Retailers should expose product, inventory, pricing, offer, and fulfillment data to agents while keeping customer identities, preferences, loyalty histories, and behavioral data under their own control.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: First-party customer data remains the retailer moat; product data becomes a commodity input to agent ranking.
insights.locator: Retailers Decide What Data Agents Can Access

insights.claim: Retailers' stances toward external agents split 42% collaborative (any agent can retrieve products), 32% selective (direct feeds to chosen agents), 6% wholly defensive (blocking), and 20% undecided.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Most retailers are opening up, which accelerates AI platforms' commerce coverage; outright blocking is rare.
insights.quote: Just 6% are wholly defensive and block agents from their data, while 20% are still deciding.
insights.locator: Most retailers surveyed are already taking a position

insights.claim: How much a retailer shares depends on destination strength: strong-destination retailers like Amazon can restrict agent access and steer shoppers to their own agents, while agent-dependent retailers must share more.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Amazon's walled-garden stance is a privilege of scale; weaker retailers will be pushed into dependency on AI platforms.
insights.quote: Retailers with a strong destination appeal can restrict access and steer consumers toward their own shopping agents, as Amazon has done.
insights.locator: How much retailers share will likely depend

insights.claim: Agent readiness is rising from crawlable product pages toward direct integrations via data feeds and APIs with live price, availability, delivery, and returns; 67% of retailers plan to enrich product data and 58% plan real-time availability within two years.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Demand tailwind for product-information, feed-management and marketplace-infrastructure vendors.
insights.quote: Sixty-seven percent of those surveyed plan to enrich their product data, and 58% plan to provide real-time availability within two years.
insights.locator: The standard for agent readiness is also rising.

insights.claim: Only 18% of retailers consider their marketplaces ready for agents, held back by fragmented legacy systems, poorly structured metadata, and lack of an integration layer.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Large readiness gap implies a multi-year modernization spend cycle and opportunity for leaders to pull ahead.
insights.quote: Only 18% of retailers consider their marketplaces ready for agents.
insights.locator: Only 18% of retailers consider their marketplaces

insights.claim: Winning agent referrals requires differentiated assortment from exclusive sellers, sharp pricing via the buy box and lower take rates on key value items, and owned fulfillment competitive on delivery, plus fast onboarding and data enrichment of long-tail sellers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Agent competition may pressure marketplace take rates on key value items and favor retailers with owned logistics.
insights.quote: sharp pricing, through the buy box and incentives such as lower take rates on key value items
insights.locator: Agents weigh assortment, price, and execution

insights.claim: Loyalty must be expressed in agent-calculable terms such as member-only prices, guaranteed delivery windows, or cash value of points, while experiential benefits agents cannot value are reserved for direct shoppers; only 14% plan to give external agents full benefits, 58% would offer a lower tier.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect tiered loyalty that deliberately disadvantages agent-routed purchases to defend the direct channel.
insights.quote: Only 14% plan to give external agents the same benefits that are available through their own channels, while 58% would offer a lower tier.
insights.locator: Loyalty and personalization must become richer

insights.claim: Personalization advantage erodes if agent-referred purchases stay anonymous, so retailers must convert them into identified, consented relationships via registration, loyalty enrollment, and preference capture.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Identity capture rate on agent-referred orders becomes a key metric for retailer data moats.
insights.quote: That advantage can erode if agent-referred purchases remain anonymous.
insights.locator: Personalization gives retailers another advantage

insights.claim: 65% of brands expect to spend more on retail media as shopping agents become common versus only 12% expecting to spend less, though growth in banner ads and sponsored search is expected to slow as agentic, social, video, and offsite formats gain.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retail media budgets look resilient but are rotating toward offsite and conversational formats.
insights.quote: 65% of brands surveyed expect to spend more as shopping agents become common, while only 12% expect to spend less
insights.locator: Retail media should monetize the engagement

insights.claim: Among retailers that have upgraded retail media data, targeting, and measurement, 65% report better campaign performance, 55% additional third-party-seller demand, and 40% higher retail media pricing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Measurement capability translates into pricing power in retail media.
insights.quote: 65% report better campaign performance, 55% report additional third-party-seller demand, and 40% report higher retail media pricing
insights.locator: Most retailers are strengthening their data

insights.claim: Agent-referred shoppers arrive with higher intent and browse less, so onsite retail media must shift to quick-engagement formats like video and user-generated content, and sponsored prompts must move into retailers' own agents as Amazon, Walmart, and bol have begun doing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Fewer page views per visit shrinks traditional onsite ad inventory; conversational ad formats are the replacement.
insights.quote: Shoppers referred by an agent come with higher intent and browse less
insights.locator: To win at the destination game

insights.claim: Retail media is the flywheel component most exposed in agentic commerce because brands want proof of incremental rather than attributed sales before investing materially; 32% of brands are very willing to join agentic pilots and 38% would with a clear business case.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retail media growth narratives hinge on incrementality proof; absent it, the highest-margin line is at risk.
insights.quote: Retail media is therefore the part of the flywheel most exposed if that proof doesn’t materialize.
insights.locator: Brands are ready to move as well.

insights.claim: 68% of retailers expect agentic commerce to have a significant or transformational effect within two years; over one-third are running pilots, 18% are deploying at scale, and 24% have not moved beyond assessment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Adoption is broad but shallow; at-scale deployers are a minority that could open a lead.
insights.quote: Sixty-eight percent of retailers surveyed expect agentic commerce to have a significant or transformational effect within two years
insights.locator: Retailers are preparing.

insights.claim: 79% of surveyed retailers and brands expect those that prepare the flywheel for agentic commerce to pull further ahead, implying a widening gap where the cost of delay rises every quarter.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect greater performance and valuation dispersion among retailers as agent adoption scales.
insights.quote: For retailers that have not started, the cost of delay rises every quarter.
insights.locator: Seventy-nine percent of the retailers and brands
